claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by a lack of nanoscale dislocation obstacles such as precipitates.
The alloy deforms primarily by relatively unimpeded dislocation slip.
Relatively unimpeded dislocation slip favors plasticity over strength.
The applicable starting material is homogeneous, single-phase, equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with minimal nanoscale second-phase particles.
Controlled aging can induce nanoscale precipitates in the CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Suitable aging conditions can produce a fine second-phase dispersion without significant grain growth.
The aging treatment will create nanoscale precipitates dispersed within the matrix.
Dislocations in the as-solid-solution state encounter low resistance because few obstacles impede their motion.
Aging-induced nanoscale precipitates will act as pinning sites for dislocations.
Precipitate pinning will increase resistance to dislocation motion and thereby enhance hardness and strength.
Aged samples will have greater yield strength and hardness than untreated solid-solution samples.
Aging-induced precipitates may reduce ductility by restricting dislocation motion.
The hypothesis is limited to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi and aging conditions that effectively generate nanoscale precipitates.
Insufficient precipitation, precipitate coarsening, or formation of deleterious phases can place the treatment outside the hypothesis's intended regime.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule treats failure to observe nanoscale precipitates as falsification of the proposed obstacle-strengthening mechanism. However, absent precipitates mean that the intended structural mediator was not successfully introduced, so this outcome primarily indicates intervention failure rather than decisively falsifying the causal hypothesis.
